curriculum.lesson_evidence: Life in the early British colony was hard: food shortages, unfamiliar climate, building shelter and illness appear in journals and official reports. These sources show colonial life; they do not replace First Nations experiences of the same years.
curriculum.scope_limit: Proposed Stage 2 NESA HSIE alignment using catalogue outcome codes (HS2-*); content-point mapping and local First Nations protocols remain pending human review.

lesson.child_mission: Life in the early British colony was hard: food shortages, unfamiliar climate, building shelter and illness appear in journals and official reports. These sources show colonial life; they do not replace First Nations experiences of the same years.
lesson.evidence_instructions: Save the independent response, specific revisions and both short-answer explanations; record oral evidence for speaking tasks.
lesson.extension: Apply the same HSIE idea to a new place or source, then compare two pieces of evidence for strength.
lesson.guided_practice:
PRACTISE BEFORE READING THE FEEDBACK
Name two hardships recorded in early colonial sources and one thing those sources usually leave out.

FEEDBACK
e.g. food shortage, disease/shelter problems; First Nations viewpoints and losses.

WATCH FOR
Using only “brave pioneer” stories without hardship or First Nations presence is one-sided.
lesson.independent_task:
INDEPENDENT EVIDENCE
From two published sources, complete a daily-life table (food, shelter, work, health). Add a column “not shown” for First Nations experiences. List sources.

Write a short reflection naming one source or idea you corrected and why.

lesson.offline_alternative: Use paper and pencil to complete the original task, then retain a photograph or short parent observation as evidence.

Parent: Marking guidance for the independent task: From two published sources, complete a daily-life table (food, shelter, work, health). Add a column “not shown” for First Nations experiences. List sources. Accept equivalent original responses that show the same skill.

Parent: Written model 1: Sample: original example using colony on new material; names a specific word, source or choice and explains its effect.

Parent: Likely misconception: Using only “brave pioneer” stories without hardship or First Nations presence is one-sided. Keep sample answers out of the child role.

Parent: Short-answer focus 1: Produce a fresh example demonstrating colony on new material (not the worked model). Explain the particular words, sources or choices that make it work.

Parent: Short-answer focus 2: Name one likely error with colony, correct it, and explain why the correction helps a reader or audience.

Parent: Marking notes: Accept original work about colony with a specific supporting detail. Reject copied model wording with no new material. / Accept a misconception, a correction, and a purpose-linked reason for colony. Reject corrections that do not change the inaccurate idea..

teach_steps.explain:
Life in the early British colony was hard: food shortages, unfamiliar climate, building shelter and illness appear in journals and official reports. These sources show colonial life; they do not replace First Nations experiences of the same years.

WHY IT MATTERS
This helps the learner base claims on sources, places and respectful community knowledge, rather than guessing from a single picture. Keep every claim linked to evidence.

HOW TO WORK
Read the worked example and name the sources, map features or community examples that carry the idea. Before looking at the correction, make your own attempt using the exact question provided. Compare your record with the feedback: did you use the same skill and show your evidence? If a detail is uncertain, identify what source you would need next. One deliberate, evidence-based revision is more useful than writing a longer answer.
